This model asks a single question: how does the number of words a typically-developing child understands change with age? Age here is a proxy for everything that happens over time ($A \rightarrow U$), not a cause in itself.

## What this model is for

This is a **reference baseline**. It exists so that the Down syndrome comprehension model, VG02, has a typically-developing curve on the same scale, fitted with the same engine and the same priors machinery, to be compared against. Every structural choice here mirrors VG02 except the population, the age anchors, the age range and the admissible measurement forms, so that a difference between the two curves is a difference between the populations rather than between two modelling approaches. It is also the comprehension counterpart of VG03, which models words spoken in the same pool.

::: {.callout-warning title="A typically-developing curve is a reference, not a target"}

Nothing in this report is a goal, a norm to be met, or a benchmark for an individual child. A typically-developing trajectory says what a different population does; it does not say what any child with Down syndrome should do, and a gap between the two curves is a description, not a deficit to be closed on a timetable. Read this model only as the comparison scale for the Down syndrome models.

:::

## Statistical model

We model the number of words understood as a bounded count out of the reference inventory. The expected proportion understood is a smooth function of age. On the logit scale that function is a straight-line developmental trend plus a Gaussian process term, which lets the curve bend away from the line by as much as the data support and no more.

Children of the same age differ far more than a simple Binomial count would allow, so the likelihood is Beta-Binomial rather than Binomial. Its dispersion parameter is itself allowed to change with age, because how much children differ from one another is not fixed across development — it is one of the things worth measuring.

The straight-line trend is not given a prior directly. Instead priors are placed on the expected proportion understood at two reference ages, which is a far more interpretable thing to have an opinion about than an intercept at age zero. Those anchors are much younger than the Down syndrome model's, because typical comprehension changes fastest across the second year. One caution on reading them: these anchors parameterise the straight-line component only. The fitted trajectory at a reference age is the anchor plus whatever the Gaussian process adds there, and in this model the process is unconstrained at the anchors — so `p_slope_low` and `p_slope_hi` are coordinates of the trend, not exact values of the fitted curve at those ages.

Only Wordbank Words & Gestures and Oxford CDI administrations contribute here. Words & Sentences comprehension values are excluded, because on that form they are production proxies rather than independently measured comprehension. This is the one substantive measurement difference between this model and its spoken counterpart, VG03, and it is why this model rests on fewer administrations over a shorter age range.

::: {.callout-important title="What this model does not do"}

This model has no study effects and no repeated-child effects. The pool contains children observed more than once, and children drawn from datasets that differ in recruitment and measurement — and one dataset contributes a large share of the rows, with nothing in the model to absorb that imbalance. **This model treats every observation as independent.** Its estimand is an administration-weighted pooled trajectory: children and datasets influence the curve in proportion to how many administrations they contribute, not equally. It is therefore a reference baseline, not the preferred account of typically-developing comprehension. For that, see VG12.

It is also fitted to a **subsample of children** rather than to the whole typically-developing pool: whole children are drawn and all of their administrations kept, so the subsample is of children, not of rows. And the pool is restricted to **English-language** administrations, because with no random effects there is nothing here to absorb between-language variation — it would be reported as if it were variation between children.

VG12 is the full-data successor, and it differs on more than data volume: it adds dataset **and** child random intercepts, anchors the Gaussian process at a reference age, and widens the reference pool beyond English. A comparison between this model and VG12 is therefore not a like-for-like check of how much the subsample cost.

:::

## Priors {#sec-priors}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

The priors above are calibrated for this population and this outcome, not inherited from the Down syndrome models: the anchor ages, the Gaussian process amplitude and the dispersion anchors were each set for a typically-developing comprehension pool. Only the length-scale prior and its month window are the shared defaults.

The low-age anchor is deliberately **not** a floor expectation. Typically-developing comprehension is already substantial in the first year, so this anchor was recalibrated upwards, off the floor, against published norms; it is not the near-zero prior the spoken models place at their low anchor. The high-age anchor is deliberately broad and favours neither a small nor a large comprehension vocabulary at that age — the table above gives both anchors' medians and ranges on the word scale. Note that the high anchor is broad regularisation rather than an encoded norm: there is no independent published comprehension norm at that age to place it against, which is why it is a registered sensitivity target — exercised on the full-data successor VG12, which carries the same anchor, rather than here. The frame also contains no comprehension observations above 25 months, so the 26-month anchor sits just past the data: do not read it as data-supported at its own age.

Dispersion follows `kappa(age) = kappa_min + exp(a_kappa + b_kappa * z)`, where `z` is standardised age. The age term is given priors at two reference ages rather than as an intercept at the pool's mean age plus a slope, so each prior is directly comparable with a per-age dispersion estimate and neither shifts meaning if the pool's age distribution changes. See `docs/models/PRIORS.md`.

Typically-developing comprehension dispersion is, unusually for these models, **flat** with age: the per-age estimates scatter without a trend across the ages this model covers. The two anchors are therefore set near-equal and only a few months apart, placed where the data are densest rather than spanning a decay, and the implied prior on the age slope of dispersion is near-symmetric about zero rather than forcing $\kappa$ to fall. The earlier single-slope parameterisation could not represent a flat dispersion curve at any setting, which is why this model uses the two-anchor form.

::: {.callout-note title="This model's dispersion is not comparable with VG12's"}

Because this model carries no random effects, its `kappa` has to absorb every source of spread at once, and its prior is calibrated **marginally** — against the pooled data. VG12's subject and dataset intercepts remove the between-child and between-study components first, so its `kappa` prior is calibrated **conditionally**, on what remains, and its anchors sit far higher for the same outcome. The two are answering different questions and their values should not be read against one another.

:::

## Prior predictive checks {#sec-prior-predictive}

These simulate vocabularies from the priors alone, before the data are seen. Read them as a plausibility test with three criteria over the typically-developing age window: simulated comprehension should already be appreciable around the first birthday rather than sitting at zero, the priors should permit rapid growth across the second year, and later trajectories should not be mechanically pinned to the inventory ceiling. A prior that fails any of these would be shaping the answer rather than permitting it. One caveat: the dispersion priors were calibrated marginally against this model's own analysis frame, so on the spread criterion these checks pass partly by construction — they test internal consistency of the specification, not independent prior plausibility.

![Trajectories drawn from the priors.](prior_samples.png){#fig-prior-samples .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Word counts simulated from those trajectories.](prior_predictions.png){#fig-prior-predictions .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Simulated counts compared with the range the observed data occupy.](prior_predictive_checks.png){#fig-prior-predictive-checks .lightbox width=640 fig-align="left"}

The table above reports, for each parameter, whether the chains agree with one another (R-hat) and how many independent samples the correlated draws are worth (ESS). This project requires R-hat no greater than 1.01 and ESS of at least 400 for **every** parameter before a fit may be reported at all, so a fit that reaches this page has already cleared those thresholds — or carries a recorded exception, disclosed above.

### Prior to posterior {#sec-contraction}

How much each prior was narrowed by the data, computed from this fit's trace rather than read off the figures above.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_prior_posterior_contraction

render_prior_posterior_contraction()
```

::: {.callout-note title="What to watch in this model"}

The understood anchors, the GP length-scale and amplitude, and the age-varying dispersion parameters. Poor behaviour in any of them would propagate directly into the comprehension trajectory and its age derivative. Compare the marginal posteriors above with the prior figures earlier in this report: a parameter whose posterior is indistinguishable from its prior has not been informed by the data, and any conclusion resting on it is a restatement of the prior. The dispersion slope `b_kappa` is worth a specific look, since the prior deliberately left the direction open — an interval straddling zero is the flat dispersion curve the calibration expected, not a failure to estimate.

Diagnostics here should also be read together with the fixed sampling seed, since the fitted frame is one particular random subsample of children.

:::

## Posterior predictions {#sec-predictions}

### Summary at selected ages

$p$ is the latent success probability — the underlying proportion of the reference inventory a child is expected to understand at a given age. $Ey$ is the expected count implied by $p$, and reflects uncertainty in the mean trajectory alone. $Y$ is a draw from the posterior predictive distribution, and reflects both that uncertainty **and** the marginal spread between same-age administrations. $Y$ is therefore much the wider of the two, and it is the one to quote when asking where a new administration — one more checklist from this pooled population, not a specific child tracked over time — might fall.

### Age derivative

![Rate of change of expected understood vocabulary with age, in words per month.](expected_learning_rate.png){#fig-expected-learning-rate .lightbox fig-align="left"}

This is the slope of the fitted age trajectory: it describes how expected vocabulary differs between children of different ages. It is **not** a within-child learning rate, and should not be read as one — most of these data are cross-sectional, so the model has little to say about any individual child's trajectory over time. Where the interval spans zero, the data do not establish the direction of change at that age.

The right-hand edge of this figure needs particular care. It sits at the last observed age, where the Gaussian process has observations on one side only, so the curve there is shaped partly by the smoother's boundary behaviour rather than by development.

![The same derivative, smoothed for presentation. The underlying numbers are unchanged.](expected_learning_rate_smoothed.png){#fig-expected-learning-rate-smoothed .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Dispersion

![How the dispersion parameter changes with age, with uncertainty intervals.](posterior_kappa.png){#fig-posterior-kappa .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Lower $\kappa$ means **greater** spread between same-age administrations relative to the mean; higher $\kappa$ means less. In this model that spread mixes between-child, between-dataset and repeat-visit variation — it is marginal count dispersion, not a between-child quantity. The direction is easy to misread, so the findings table above restates it as a variance inflation factor, where a larger number means a wider spread. This is the model whose dispersion prior expected no trend with age, so the thing to check here is whether the fitted curve is flat and whether its interval is wide enough to admit a trend anyway.

## Expected vocabulary by month {#sec-monthly}

A finer companion to the table above: one row per whole month, with the expected count, the range a new administration might fall in, and the probability of scoring below given thresholds. The `n_obs` column gives the number of observations near each age, which is the honest guide to where these expectations rest on data and where they rest on the model. Read a row with a small or zero `n_obs` as the model interpolating, not as evidence — and note that in this model the counts fall away sharply in the upper part of the range, well before the table ends.

## Limits {#sec-limits}

- **A reference, not a target.** This curve describes a different population. It is not a norm any individual child is expected to meet, and it is not an intervention goal.
- **The query grid runs past the evidence, so reporting is capped.** Comprehension observations stop at 25 months, and this outcome's reporting cap trims the 27- and 30-month query ages, which would otherwise be pure extrapolation. The monthly table stops at the last observation and should be preferred.
- **No hierarchy.** Study and repeated-child structure are absent, so uncertainty here is not a fair estimate of uncertainty about a new child, and one dominant contributing dataset has nothing to absorb it. Use VG12 for that.
- **A subsample, and English only.** The fit uses a random subsample of children from the typically-developing pool, restricted to English-language administrations. VG12 uses the full pool and a wider language scope, so it is the model to use when coverage matters.
- **Age is not a mechanism.** Everything reported is an association with age, not an effect of it.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** No typically-developing child in this pool was assessed on the full inventory: the forms used here are shorter, and their counts are treated as nested inside the common scale so that typically-developing and Down syndrome counts are comparable. It is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat.
- **Comprehension is measured on fewer forms than production.** Words & Sentences comprehension is excluded as a production proxy, so this model rests on a smaller and younger pool than VG03 and the two are not equally well supported at the same ages.
- **Dispersion is not comparable with VG12's**, for the marginal-versus-conditional reason given in the priors section.
- **The dispersion floor is not identified.** With a flat dispersion curve, any split of the level between the floor `kappa_min` and the age term fits equally well, so the floor is a nuisance parameter here rather than a finding; the anchors carry the level.
- **No sensitivity variants and no parameter-recovery check are registered for this model.** It is a descriptive baseline rather than a gated estimand, so the absence of those checks is by design — but it means the results here have not been stress-tested the way the models of record have.
